resources.string: Tetto answers one question for each thing you put a cap on: how much can you still spend, and until when. This guide says what each part of the screen is for, and the few things worth knowing that a screen cannot say out loud.

One sentence first, then a tile for each cap. The sentence speaks for all of them at once: everything under its cap and the one closest to it, or a cap that went over and when it starts again. Each tile speaks for one.
An example, on a %1$s: Coffee well under its cap, with something in reserve; Eating out spending ahead of the days.

The large figure is what you can still spend in this period: the cap and its reserve, less what you spent. Under it, the cap and the period’s last day: “until Sunday” counts Sunday too. Past the cap, the figure says how much over, in words as well as in colour.

The bar fills with what you spent. The thin line across it is today, as far into the period as the days are. A bar well past the line is spending ahead of the days, and changes colour to say so: early in a period it has some room (a day of a week, a week of a month), less and less as the days run out. It is not an alarm: on a period’s last day a full bar is right on time.
On a cap of a week or longer with a few days still to go: about how much a day keeps you under it until the end.

With many caps, the list shows more of them on a screen: one cap a row, its figure beside its name. The pace and the reserve are then in the cap’s sheet, a long press away. The choice is in Settings, under Appearance.

At the end of the screen: what you added to your caps in your month so far, and in the month before, to set against your salary. Your month starts on the day chosen in Settings, payday if you like. Beside it, what your caps are worth in a month, about: a week’s cap for the month’s days, a year’s for a twelfth. Only what you add in Tetto counts: bills and anything you do not add stay out.
Left open across midnight, the screen turns the day by itself: a period that ends closes, and the next one opens.
A period, the reserve and forgiveness
Each cap runs on its own period: a day, a week, a month or a year. When a period ends, what it left over is set aside, what it overspent is settled, and the next period starts whole.

An example: four weeks of a %1$s coffee cap. What the first week left over carried the second past its cap; the third spent more than its reserve could cover, and the rest was forgiven. The fourth starts whole.

What a period leaves over goes to the cap’s reserve, up to one period’s cap, so a few quiet weeks never turn a cap into a budget of its own. The reserve counts in what is left, and its chip on the tile says how much there is.

An overspend takes from the reserve first. What the reserve cannot cover is forgiven when the period ends: the next period starts at its full cap, never in debt. A bad week stays one bad week. The day a period starts again, the sentence on top says how the last one ended: forgiven, covered by the reserve, or what it left to it.
A week starts on your phone’s first day of the week, a month on the 1st, a year on that day of January. Both can change in Settings: a month from the 27th, say, for a salary paid on the 27th.

A trip, a festival, a move: a cap can run once, between two dates of its own, instead of every day, week, month or year. It keeps no reserve and never starts again. Its mark, its pace and its room ahead of the days follow its own length. The day after its last, the sentence on top says how it went; its tile then waits at the end, quieter, to run again with new dates or to be deleted.

A new amount counts at once, in the period under way, and a reserve larger than it comes down to it: a reserve is never more than one period’s cap. A new period that holds this one’s days takes its spends. One that starts later, a week turned into days on a Thursday, closes the days already past on their share of the cap, and only what you spend from its first day counts in it.

Nothing runs at midnight with the screen off. The first time Tetto is read after a period ends (the app, a widget, the reminder) it closes every period that ended since, in order. After weeks away, the empty ones are counted together, and the reserve stops at its limit.

A closed period never changes again: its spends can no longer be corrected, so the reserve never moves behind your back. A cap’s sheet keeps the last three, one line each, to say where the reserve came from.
The numpad, and fixing a spend

A spend is an amount, in one cap, now: no date, no note, no category to look for. The cap you touched is the category. Once a cap has a few spends, the amounts you use most wait above the keys, each added in one touch, until you type something else.
An example: %1$s typed on a cap with %2$s left, and under the amount what it would leave.

Before you add, the line under the amount says what the spend would leave while it fits, how much over once it does not, and “still over” when the cap was over already. It is the only warning Tetto gives, at the one moment it can still change anything.

After a spend is added, the figure rolls to its new value and a message offers to undo it, for as long as your phone’s accessibility settings ask. A wrong amount noticed later can still be fixed: every spend of the period under way is in the cap’s sheet, to correct or to delete.

Behind the arrow by a cap’s name, or a long press on its tile: this period’s figures as a receipt, its spends with the day and time of each, a refund for money that comes back (a return, a friend’s share), the last periods in one line each, and the cap itself, to change or delete. A refund gives back at most what the period spent. Clearing the reserve there starts a cap afresh.
The decimal key is your language’s, and a currency without cents has none. Each key ticks as your phone’s keyboard does; your phone’s own touch feedback setting turns it off.

«At a glance» holds your caps, as many as its size allows, each with what is left and a slim bar. «In words» holds one cap in a ring, with what is left in words: the cap you choose, or the one closest to its cap. Neither ever scrolls: what does not fit is counted. Touch and hold one for its own settings: its background and colour, its opacity, its caps.
A spend without opening the app
A touch on a cap on a widget opens the numpad over the home screen: two touches and the amount, and you are back where you were. A long press on Tetto’s icon offers your first four caps the same way.
A widget says “until Sunday”, never how many hours are left: it is redrawn after every spend and at midnight, not every minute, so a countdown would soon be wrong.
A widget can show no amount at all, for a home screen others can see. The bars, the ring, the names and the days stay, and a cap over still says so in words.

Turned on in Settings, one notification in the evening asks whether there is anything to add, and only on a day with no spend added. It comes near the time you chose, not to the minute: Tetto asks Android for no exact alarm, so the phone can save its battery, and some phones hold it back a little longer.
Tetto has no internet permission at all: it sends nothing, to anyone. Your caps and your spends are kept on this phone.

They leave it only in a file you save (a backup, to restore here or on another phone, or your spends as a CSV for a spreadsheet) or in Android’s own backup, if it is turned on: that copy is Android’s, not Tetto’s.
A backup file is not encrypted: keep it where you keep other private files. Restoring one replaces the caps on this phone, after it has said what it holds and what it replaces.

Tetto can also lock itself behind the phone’s own fingerprint, face or screen lock, when it opens and after a minute away; the recent apps then show no picture of it. It keeps no secret of its own: the phone checks, and Tetto only hears yes or no.
Tetto keeps no ledger: no history to scroll, no statistics or charts, no accounts, no income, no notes or tags on a spend. That is what keeps a spend to two touches, and the screen on one question.
If you want every movement kept for good, with balances and charts of where your money went, you want an expense tracker: another kind of app, made for that.
Caps of different periods do not add up: a week of coffee and a year of presents make no sum worth reading, so there is none.
An overspend on one cap is never paid from another: the reserve and forgiveness are the whole mechanism, so each cap keeps meaning what you set.
No warning at 80%, no message when you go over: the numpad says what a spend will leave before you add it.
Every amount in one currency. Changing it in Settings relabels your figures and never converts them.
Example of the numpad: %1$s typed on %2$s, which has %3$s left. Under the amount: %4$s
